summary:
Lunar Landing Site Navigator is an interactive web platform designed to evaluate and compare potential lunar landing sites by analyzing solar illumination and Earth visibility over real lunar topography. Built with a Python/FastAPI backend and a custom 2D/3D web interface, the application combines astronomical ephemerides with Digital Elevation Models (DEM) from NASA’s Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA).

To address the challenge of operating in extreme lunar environments (especially near the Lunar South Pole) our tool calculates 360° horizon obstruction profiles alongside the apparent trajectories of the Sun and Earth. Users can explore custom coordinates, dates, and mission durations through a 2D horizon panorama, a multi-site comparison heatmap, and two interactive 3D visualizations (an orbital lunar globe with dynamic shadows and a first-person surface view), plus a step-by-step educational mode.

As NASA’s Artemis and CLPS missions prepare for sustained lunar exploration, accurately predicting power availability and communication blackouts is vital for mission safety, engineering planning, and public science outreach.
details:
HOW IT WORKS & WHAT IT DOES

Lunar Landing Site Navigator is a full-stack web application that evaluates potential lunar landing sites by simulating solar illumination and Direct-to-Earth (DTE) communication windows across real lunar topography. When a user selects a candidate landing site (such as Shackleton Rim, Malapert Massif, or Apollo historical sites) or enters custom coordinates, dates, and mission duration, our backend calculates the apparent azimuth and elevation trajectories of the Sun and Earth alongside a 360° horizon elevation profile derived from NASA LOLA Digital Elevation Models (DEM). The platform then computes key mission metrics (solar illumination percentage, longest continuous lunar night, maximum solar elevation, Earth visibility percentage, and maximum communication blackout) and renders them across interactive 2D and 3D views.

BENEFITS & EXPECTED IMPACT

Planning lunar surface operations requires balancing power generation with uninterrupted telemetry. Our tool translates complex planetary elevation datasets into intuitive visual insights for mission planners, researchers, and students. Additionally, our built-in step-by-step Educational Mode ("Modo Educativo") lowers the barrier to entry so students and the general public can understand why landing near the Lunar South Pole poses unique geometric and thermal challenges.

TOOLS, LANGUAGES & SOFTWARE USED

• Backend: Python, FastAPI, Uvicorn, and NumPy for astronomical ephemerides, ray-marching horizon profiles, and automated testing (pytest).

• Frontend: HTML5, CSS3 (styled with NASA-inspired USWDS typography: Inter, Public Sans, and DM Mono), and Vanilla JavaScript.

• Custom Visualization Engine: Built from scratch using native HTML5 2D/3D Canvas rendering (vista3d.js) without heavy external 3D game engines, ensuring fast performance in any standard web browser.

• Collaboration & Workflow: Git, GitHub, and Visual Studio Code.

CREATIVITY & KEY FACTORS CONSIDERED

Instead of limiting users to static tables or heavy desktop GIS software, we combined a fast 360° horizon-method solver with synchronized dual 3D perspectives: an orbital lunar globe showing real-time terrain shadows and a first-person surface view ("from the astronaut's eyes") looking out at crater rims, paired with a multi-site comparison heatmap. Key engineering factors included extremely low solar incidence angles at the Lunar South Pole, long shadows cast by distant crater walls, simultaneous line-of-sight constraints to Earth, customizable time steps, and clear visual hierarchy.
